Maladaptive Strategies.value: News reports about events similar to what happened to me
wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed

Negative Appraisals.value: I should have protected others and I failed
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

vignette:
Priya had been in the market that day because the children needed new shoes. She remembered the heat, the press of bodies, and then the sound—a roar that turned the world into rubble. For hours afterward, she had dug through debris, calling for the two little girls she had been guiding. She found one alive; the other did not make it. In the weeks that followed, as the conflict escalated and she managed to leave that country, a single thought lodged itself in her mind like a shard: *I should have been able to protect them. I failed.*

Now, eight years later, Priya worked as a school counselor in a quiet American suburb. But the shard had grown roots. She had come to believe that the failure was not an event but a truth about who she was: a weak person, someone who crumbles when it matters most. That belief had hollowed out the work she once loved. She used to think of herself as steady, someone other people leaned on. Now she felt like a shell, and she was certain that anyone who looked closely would see she was no longer capable of doing the things that had defined her—not as a counselor, not as a wife, not as a friend.

The triggers came disguised as ordinary things. News reports about distant conflicts sent her heart racing; she had not watched a broadcast in years. She would turn off the radio the moment a headline mentioned a bombing, even if it was a completely different country. Her husband had learned to mute the television when she entered the room. She also avoided public transport entirely. The crowded bus reminded her of bodies pressing in, of not being able to see an exit. She drove everywhere, even for short trips, even when it meant circling for parking or spending money they did not really have. And she wore concealing clothing—long sleeves, loose pants, a scarf she could pull up—even on hot days. She was not cold. She was certain that if anyone noticed her, really looked at her, they would see the weakness. She had become invisible on purpose.

The consequences crept up slowly. At school, she found herself unable to join conversations in the staff lounge when a teacher talked about a news segment. She excused herself, saying she felt unwell. She stopped taking the shuttle to district meetings because she could not bear the enclosed space with strangers. Her principal noticed she seemed distracted. Her colleagues began to treat her gently, as if she were fragile. That only confirmed her belief.

Last month, during a lunch group with middle schoolers, a boy mentioned a video he had seen online—something about a conflict overseas. Priya felt her chest tighten, her vision narrow. She told the group she needed a glass of water and walked to the bathroom, where she sat on the floor for ten minutes, shaking. That was the moment she realized she could no longer manage this alone. She had not told her husband the full story; she did not want him to see how broken she was. But after that incident, she called a therapist who specialized in trauma.

What frightened her most was not the memory itself, but the possibility that she was right—that she really was too weak to help anyone, that she would never be the person she used to be. Yet a smaller, quieter part of her wondered if maybe, just maybe, there was a way to carry the memory without letting it define every step she took. That was why she walked into the office that first day, her scarf wrapped tightly around her shoulders, hoping to be seen without being exposed.
